blocks.text: 1. Tanh
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444652457-64192146.png

Sigmoid's not-zero-centered weakness, the previous topic's closing limitation, left a genuine gap for improvement. Tanh directly fixes exactly this one specific problem, while remaining a close mathematical cousin of sigmoid overall.
Tanh shares sigmoid's overall S-shape, but with a genuinely different output range, a difference that turns out to matter considerably for how well a network actually trains in practice.
2. Tanh's Mathematics
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444652458-431358676.png
Tanh takes any real number as input, positive or negative, and squashes it into a smooth S-shaped curve too, exactly the same overall family of shape already covered in the Sigmoid topic.

The key difference is that tanh's output ranges from negative 1 to positive 1, instead of sigmoid's 0-to-1 range, a genuinely different span that directly addresses the not-zero-centered problem already covered in the previous topic.
3. Directly Fixing the Zero-Centered Weakness
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444785446-550138760.png

This directly solves sigmoid's not-zero-centered weakness, already covered in the previous topic. Tanh's output spreads symmetrically around zero, meaning negative inputs genuinely produce negative outputs, not merely smaller positive outputs the way sigmoid always would.

This connects to the training-speed concern already raised in the Sigmoid topic. This symmetry genuinely helps training converge somewhat faster in practice, a concrete, measurable improvement over sigmoid despite the two functions sharing so much of their underlying mathematical shape.
4. The Mathematical Relationship to Sigmoid
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444785448-903510288.png

This connects back to sigmoid's own mathematics, already covered fully in the Sigmoid topic. Tanh is, mathematically, genuinely just a rescaled and shifted version of sigmoid, not an entirely separate, unrelated function.

It shares the exact same fundamental S-shape, simply stretched to span negative 1 to positive 1 instead of 0 to 1, a direct mathematical relationship worth understanding clearly rather than treating tanh and sigmoid as two unrelated topics.
5. Still Facing the Vanishing Gradient Problem

blocks.alt: Still Facing the Vanishing Gradient Problem
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444785448-785003619.png

The vanishing gradient problem, already covered in genuine depth in the Sigmoid topic, still applies here too. Tanh's curve also flattens out for very large positive or very large negative inputs, and its gradient in those flattened regions also becomes extremely small.

This shared weakness is genuinely not fixed by the zero-centering improvement covered earlier in this topic. Tanh is not a full solution to the vanishing gradient problem, only a partial improvement over sigmoid, a genuinely important distinction worth keeping clear.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Do not mistake tanh's zero-centering fix for a solution to the vanishing gradient problem itself. Both weaknesses covered for sigmoid in the previous topic are genuinely separate issues, and tanh only addresses one of the two.

blocks.text: 6. A Steeper Gradient Near Zero
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444785449-830927012.png

One genuine, measurable advantage tanh has over sigmoid is that its gradient near an input of zero is steeper than sigmoid's own gradient at that same point, a direct mathematical consequence of tanh's wider, negative-1-to-1 output range.

This steeper gradient can, in practice, lead to somewhat faster early training, a real, concrete benefit worth weighing alongside tanh's shared vanishing gradient weakness already covered in the previous section.
7. Historical Usage

This connects back to the second AI winter, already covered in the History of Deep Learning topic. Tanh was a genuinely common hidden-layer activation choice throughout that era, generally preferred over sigmoid specifically because of the zero-centering advantage already covered earlier in this topic.
This remained true before ReLU, covered in the very next topic in this module, eventually became the far more dominant default choice for hidden layers across most modern network architectures.
8. Where Tanh Still Fits Today
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444785449-344549807.png

Recurrent Neural Networks and LSTMs, both covered in their own dedicated modules later in this course, still commonly use tanh, remaining a genuinely standard, common choice specifically within that particular architecture family.

Plain feedforward hidden layers, the kind covered throughout this course so far, have largely replaced tanh with ReLU and its variants, covered in the very next topic, given the more complete solution to the vanishing gradient problem those alternatives actually provide.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Tanh Is Genuinely Right

A hidden layer inside a Recurrent Neural Network or LSTM, both covered in their own modules considerably later in this course, still calls for tanh as a genuinely standard, common choice specifically within that architecture family.

A hidden layer in a plain, deep feedforward network generally calls for ReLU and its variants instead, covered in the very next topic, given the more complete practical solution to the vanishing gradient problem those alternatives actually offer over tanh.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly compares sigmoid and tanh on the exact same inputs, illustrating the zero-centering difference covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

def tanh(x):
    return np.tanh(x)

test_inputs = np.array([-3, -1, 0, 1, 3])

print("Input | Sigmoid output | Tanh output")
for x in test_inputs:
    sig_out = sigmoid(x)
    tanh_out = tanh(x)
    print(f"  {x:4.0f}  |     {sig_out:.4f}     |   {tanh_out:.4f}")

print("\nNotice sigmoid's output is always positive, never crossing zero,")
print("while tanh's output genuinely crosses into negative territory for negative inputs")

sigmoid_mean = sigmoid(test_inputs).mean()
tanh_mean = tanh(test_inputs).mean()
print(f"\nMean output across these inputs, sigmoid: {sigmoid_mean:.3f}, tanh: {tanh_mean:.3f}")
print("Tanh's mean sits much closer to zero, exactly the zero-centering advantage covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example directly illustrates the zero-centering difference covered throughout this topic: sigmoid's outputs cluster entirely above zero, while tanh's outputs spread symmetrically around it.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Tanh directly fixes sigmoid's not-zero-centered weakness while remaining a close mathematical cousin.
It squashes any real number into a smooth S-shaped curve too, but output ranges from -1 to 1, not 0 to 1.
Its output spreads symmetrically around zero, with negative inputs genuinely producing negative outputs.
Tanh is mathematically just a rescaled and shifted version of sigmoid, sharing the same fundamental shape.
It still faces the vanishing gradient problem for extreme inputs, only a partial improvement over sigmoid.
Its steeper gradient near zero can lead to somewhat faster early training than sigmoid.
Tanh was a genuinely common hidden-layer choice before ReLU became the far more dominant default.
It remains a standard choice in Recurrent Neural Networks and LSTMs, covered later in this course.
Next up: ReLU, the function that finally provided a far more complete solution to the vanishing gradient problem.
